execute: echo: true eval: true freeze: true editor: visual --- # Caveat emptor ## Caveats I will be showing you what you *can* do, not what you *should* do
. . . Creating LLM tools for phenotyping is relatively easy. Creating tools that are trusted, improve the quality of research, and provide a good user experience is the hard part.
. . . Choice of model undoubtedly matters. But not clear which model is best, by how much, or for which task.
. . . System prompts and user input can also have a dramatic impact on the results.
. . . Closed-weight cloud-based models show performance drift, making validation even harder. ## More caveats Reliance on LLM tooling in OHDSI can increase barrier to entry, especially if tools are tied to specific providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc)
. . . And even more so if tools need access to other paid-for APIs (e.g. clinical resources) ## Even more caveats Low quality health research is prevalent
. . . Reproducibility crisis in health research
. . . LLM integration can go both ways. Increasing risk of OMOP-slop vs additional context and double-checking. # Working with LLMs from R ## ellmer We'll be using the `ellmer` R package for interacting with LLMs.
. . . Provides a simple interface for working with LLMs in a consistent manner.
. . . Building on `ellmer`, we can add model-agnostic support with users choosing the model to use. ## Unstructured chat `ellmer` supports various popular providers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) chat <- chat_anthropic() chat <- chat_deepseek() chat <- chat_google_gemini() chat <- chat_mistral() chat <- chat_openai() ``` :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellmer::models_google_gemini() |> dplyr::pull("id") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "antigravity-preview-05-2026" [2] "antigravity-preview-09-2026" [3] "antigravity-preview-latest" [4] "deep-research-max-preview-04-2026" [5] "deep-research-preview-04-2026" [6] "deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025" [7] "gemini-2.5-computer-use-preview-10-2025" [8] "gemini-2.5-flash" [9] "gemini-2.5-flash-image" [10] "gemini-2.5-flash-lite" [11] "gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts" [12] "gemini-2.5-pro" [13] "gemini-2.5-pro-preview-tts" [14] "gemini-3-flash-preview" [15] "gemini-3-pro-image" [16] "gemini-3-pro-image-preview" [17] "gemini-3.1-flash-image" [18] "gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview" [19] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite" [20] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image" [21] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview" [22] "gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview" [23] "gemini-3.1-pro-preview" [24] "gemini-3.1-pro-preview-customtools" [25] "gemini-3.5-flash" [26] "gemini-3.5-flash-lite" [27] "gemini-3.5-transcribe" [28] "gemini-3.6-flash" [29] "gemini-3.7-flash" [30] "gemini-3.8-flash" [31] "gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts" [32] "gemini-3.8-flash-tts" [33] "gemini-4-argon" [34] "gemini-flash-latest" [35] "gemini-flash-lite-latest" [36] "gemini-nano-banana-2.1" [37] "gemini-omni-1.1-flash" [38] "gemini-omni-flash-preview" [39] "gemini-pro-latest" [40] "gemini-robotics-er-2-preview" [41] "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it" [42] "gemma-4-31b-it" [43] "lyria-3-clip-preview" [44] "lyria-3-pro-preview" [45] "lyria-3.5" [46] "nano-banana-pro-preview" ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat Similarly, we can run open-weight models locally via Ollama: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat <- chat_ollama() ``` :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellmer::models_ollama() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` id created_at size capabilities 1 MedGemma:4b 2026-10-14 3338942556 completion,vision 2 gemma3:4b 2026-10-14 3350272403 completion,vision 3 qwen2.5:0.5b 2026-10-14 397821319 completion,tools 4 gemma3:1b 2026-10-14 806067407 completion ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat I'm going to be using local MedGemma 4B today. You can choose a model you have access to. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) library(dplyr) library(PhenotypeR) system_prompt <- "You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based." chat_medgemma <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt ) chat_medgemma ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ── system ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat We can work with a simple, unstructured, chat. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension clinical presentation is defined by elevated blood pressure, with a combination of upper limb and/or lower limb measurements exceeding thresholds (e.g., >140/90 mmHg for stage 2 hypertension). Clinical findings may include headaches, dizziness, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, chest pain, visual disturbances, and edema. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What are the demographics of people presenting with hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension incidence and prevalence vary by demographics including age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and geographic location. Risk factors often include obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, tobacco use, and excessive alcohol consumption. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat Bad idea: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What clinical codes should I use to identify hypertension in my OMOP CDM?") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` For hypertension in OMOP CDM, I would suggest using the following clinical codes, with appropriate nuance based on your specific data sources and goals: * **ICD-10:** * I10 - Essential (primary) hypertension. * I11 - Secondary hypertension due to renal artery stenosis. * I12 - Secondary hypertension due to left ventricular dysfunction. * I13 - Secondary hypertension due to kidney disease. * I15 - Other secondary hypertension. * I17 - Hypertensive heart disease - systolic. * I18 - Hypertensive heart disease - diastolic. * I25 - Hypertensive disease. * I42 - Hypertension due to kidney disease, unspecified. * I43 - Hypertension due to other kidney disease. * I65.1 - Hypertensive heart disease. Note the difference between I17 and I65.1. I65.1 is a *diagnosis*, I17 is a *condition*. * **SNOMED CT:** * 22041009 - Hypertension * 23066007 - Hypertension due to kidney disease * 23066006 - Hypertension due to left ventricular dysfunction * 23066005 - Hypertension due to renal artery stenosis * 23066004 - Hypertension due to kidney disease, unspecified * 23066003 - Hypertension due to heart failure (note: heart failure is linked to hypertension) * **CPT:** Although CPT codes are primarily for procedures, some related codes might be present in some circumstances (e.g. 99214 for office visits, but these are not hypertension codes). **Important Considerations:** * **Specificity:** Choose the most specific code available. For instance, if the diagnosis code indicates renal artery stenosis, use code I11. Use I17 if a general hypertensive heart disease diagnosis is present. * **Context:** Consider the clinical context. If the hypertension is secondary to another condition, use the appropriate secondary hypertension code. * **Data Quality:** Clean and consistent coding is essential for accurate analysis. * **Definitions:** Be aware of the official definitions of each code (ICD-10, SNOMED CT, etc.) for accurate characterization of the cohort. * **SNOMED CT:** SNOMED CT is highly recommended for its superior coding capabilities, especially when using the OMOP CDM. Always refer to the official documentation for the specific codes you are using to ensure accurate and consistent implementation. ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat Instead of allowing freedom in output, we can instead force results to be returned in a specific structured format ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension", type = type_object( typical_symptoms = type_string("summarise typical symptoms"), confirmatory_test = type_string("summarise what test result would confirm diagnosis"), disqualifying_diagnoses = type_string("summarise what alternative diagnoses need to be ruled out") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $typical_symptoms [1] "Headache, dizziness, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, chest pain, visual disturbances, edema" $confirmatory_test [1] "Elevated blood pressure measurements (upper and lower limbs)" $disqualifying_diagnoses [1] "Hypertensive heart disease (I17 vs I65.1), kidney disease (I13, I42, I43), left ventricular dysfunction (I12), renal artery stenosis (I11), other secondary causes (I15), stage 2 hypertension (upper/lower limb > 140/90 mmHg) " ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat We can force results to be integers/ numbers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "What are the demographics of people presenting with hypertension", type = type_object( average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer("What is the average age at diagnosis?"), proportion_male = type_number("What proportion (between 0 and 1) of patients diagnosed with hypertension are male?") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $average_age_at_diagnosis [1] 60 $proportion_male [1] 0.5239868 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat But remember, even with the same model you can get different results! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 54 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 40 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 45 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 40 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 58 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 52 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 53 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 58 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 40 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat We can set temperature to zero and add a seed to get closer to reproducibility. (This generally works better for local models than when working with cloud models.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt, params = params(temperature = 0, seed = 42) ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 ``` ::: ::: # Integrating LLMs with PhenotypeR ## Designed first for open-weight locally-hosted models - Available to all of the OHDSI community
. . . - Smoother package development (easy to implement, cheaper, and straightforward to test)
. . . - Easy to switch to using frontier models (and see if they are worth the extra cost).
. . . - But 6+ months behind "state-of-the-art". (Although allows us to learn from experience of others) ## Human-in-the-loop - Designed to support the human phenotyper, not automate them away.
. . . - All LLM-generated artefacts can be inspected, reviewed, and edited.
. . . - Main use of LLM is to provide additional context making it easier to double-check results ## Phenotyping tasks > "A problem well stated is a problem half solved." > > Charles F. Kettering (1876 – 1958)
. . . Nowadays, a problem well stated is a problem 95% solved. ## Phenotyping tasks Started with lower-stakes, human-in-the-loop, phenotyping tasks: - Drafting clinical descriptions . . . - Reviewing codes included that led to cohort inclusion . . . - Contextualising PhenotypeR results . . . Higher-risk tasks currently out-of-scope: - Searching for codes. . . . - Creating cohort logic. . . . - End-to-end phenotyping # Clinical descriptions ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clinicalDescriptionSpecification() |> listviewer::jsonedit() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyClinicalDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, "hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting clinical description for hypertension using MedGemma:4b ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $hypertension $hypertension$metadata $hypertension$metadata$phenotype_name [1] "hypertension" $hypertension$metadata$version [1] "1.0" $hypertension$metadata$created_by [1] "MedGemma:4b" $hypertension$metadata$created_date [1] "2026-10-20" $hypertension$metadata$last_edited_by [1] "N/A" $hypertension$metadata$last_edited_date [1] "2026-10-20" $hypertension$metadata$source_of_information [1] "MedGemma:4b" $hypertension$clinical_profile $hypertension$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms [1] "Hypertension is a chronic medical condition characterised by elevated blood pressure in the arteries. Other terms used include high blood pressure, arterial hypertension, and grade 1 hypertension." $hypertension$clinical_profile$clinical_presentation_and_symptoms [1] "The clinical presentation of hypertension is often asymptomatic, with many people not experiencing any noticeable symptoms until complications develop. When symptoms are present, they can include severe headaches, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, chest pain, irregular heartbeat, or vision changes. Some individuals may experience dizziness or fatigue." $hypertension$clinical_profile$assessment_diagnosis [1] "Hypertension is typically diagnosed through repeated blood pressure measurements taken during routine check-ups or when symptoms are present. Elevated blood pressure on multiple occasions is required for diagnosis. Diagnostic tests used to assess hypertension include ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), which measures blood pressure over a 24-hour period, and home blood pressure monitoring. Other laboratory tests may be performed to assess kidney function and cardiovascular risk." $hypertension$clinical_profile$therapeutic_plan_treatment [1] "The initial management of hypertension typically involves lifestyle modifications, such as reducing sodium intake, increasing potassium intake, engaging in regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight, and limiting alcohol consumption. If lifestyle modifications are insufficient, antihypertensive medications may be prescribed. These medications may include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, beta-blockers, or calcium channel blockers. The choice of medication depends on the individual's blood pressure level, other medical conditions, and tolerance to medication. Treatment goals are usually a target blood pressure (generally less than 140/90 mmHg for many patients)." $hypertension$clinical_profile$complications_prognosis [1] "Untreated hypertension can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular disease, stroke, heart failure, kidney failure, and vision loss. The prognosis for individuals with hypertension depends on the severity of the condition and the presence of other risk factors. Regular monitoring of blood pressure and adherence to treatment are essential for improving outcomes. Short term prognosis involves regular check ups and blood pressure monitoring. Medium term prognosis involves controlling blood pressure through lifestyle and medications. Longer term prognosis involves maintaining blood pressure under control to prevent major complications." $hypertension$clinical_profile$disqualifiers [1] "Differential diagnoses for hypertension include secondary hypertension, which is high blood pressure caused by an underlying medical condition, such as kidney disease, sleep apnea, or hyperaldosteronism. Other conditions that may be considered include white coat hypertension (elevated blood pressure in a clinical setting but normal blood pressure at home), masked hypertension (normal blood pressure in a clinical setting but elevated blood pressure at home), and pheochromocytoma (a rare tumor of the adrenal gland that causes episodic high blood pressure). These conditions are considered when blood pressure readings are inconsistent or unexplained." $hypertension$clinical_profile$epidemiology [1] "Hypertension is more prevalent in older adults, African Americans, and individuals with a family history of hypertension. It is also more common in men than women, particularly before menopause. Modifiable risk factors include high sodium intake, obesity, physical inactivity, and excessive alcohol consumption. Non-modifiable risk factors include age, race/ethnicity, and family history. Common comorbidities include diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease, and stroke." ``` ::: ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, c("Primary hypertension", "Secondary hypertension", "Resistant hypertension")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Primary hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Primary hypertension, essential hypertension, malignant hypertension" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Secondary hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Secondary hypertension is high blood pressure that is not caused by primary hypertension, also known as essential hypertension. Other terms used in the medical literature include secondary essential hypertension, resistant hypertension, and refractory hypertension." ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Resistant hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure that remains above target levels despite the use of three different classes of antihypertensive medications, including a diuretic, at optimal doses, and without other identifiable causes of secondary hypertension. Other synonyms include uncontrolled hypertension, refractory hypertension, and resistant hypertension." ``` ::: ::: ## Extra context: data source descriptions Data partner descriptions can be used to provide extra context ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyDataSourceDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: # Reviewing codes ## Reviewing codes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(omock) library(CohortConstructor) library(PhenotypeR) library(gt) cdm <- mockCdmFromDataset(datasetName = "synpuf-1k_5.4", source = "duckdb") cdm$hypertension <- conceptCohort(cdm, list(hypertension = c(320128, 312648, 201826, 313217)), name = "hypertension") code_diag <- codelistDiagnostics(cdm$hypertension) reviewCohortConcepts(chat_medgemma, code_diag, hypertension_cd) |> select(standard_concept, source_concept_name, score, explanation) |> gt() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

chat_medgemma_fresh$set_turns(list()) chat_medgemma_fresh$set_system_prompt(system_prompt) age_task <- Task$new( dataset = age_benchmark, solver = generate_structured( solver_chat = Tool calling ## Tool calling We can incorporate tool calling. But note we can't use them directly with structured chat. We first have to use chat for the tool to be run, and then extract out into structured chat. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) library(httr2) chat <- chat_google_gemini(model = "gemini-4-argon") search_hecate_standard_concepts <- function(query) { req <- request("https://hecate.pantheon-hds.com/api/search_standard") |> req_url_query(q = query) resp <- req_perform(req) resp_body_string(resp) } hecate_tool <- tool( search_hecate_standard_concepts, name = "search_hecate", description = "Search the OHDSI Hecate semantic search engine for standard concepts", arguments = list( query = type_string( "The medical term or condition related to my search.", required = TRUE ) ) ) chat$register_tool(hecate_tool) chat$chat( "Use the Hecate tool to search for 'hypertension' and list all returned concepts." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ◯ [tool call] search_hecate(query = "hypertension") ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ● #> Here is the summary of the NICE approach to diagnosing hypertension: --- ### 1. Initial Clinic Blood Pressure Measurement * **Check pulse first:** Palpate the radial or brachial pulse before measuring BP. If the pulse is irregular (suspected atrial fibrillation), measure BP **manually** using direct auscultation over the brachial artery, rather than an automated device. * **Both arms:** When considering a diagnosis, measure BP in both arms. If the difference in readings between arms is **more than 15 mmHg**, repeat the measurements. If the difference remains more than 15 mmHg on the second measurement, measure subsequent BPs in the arm with the **higher** reading. * **Multiple readings:** If the first clinic reading is **≥ 140/90 mmHg**, take a second reading during the consultation. If the second reading is substantially different from the first, take a third reading. Record the **lower of the last two measurements** as the clinic blood pressure. --- ### 2. Confirming the Diagnosis (ABPM vs. HBPM) If the clinic blood pressure is between **140/90 mmHg and 180/120 mmHg**, do not diagnose hypertension based on the clinic reading alone. Instead: * **Gold Standard – ABPM:** Offer **Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM)** to confirm the diagnosis. * *Protocol:* Ensure at least 2 measurements per hour are taken during the person's usual waking hours (e.g., between 08:00 and 22:00). Use the average value of at least 14 measurements taken during waking hours to confirm the diagnosis. * **Alternative – HBPM:** If a person is unable to tolerate ABPM, offer **Home Blood Pressure Monitoring (HBPM)** as an alternative. * *Protocol:* For each BP recording, take two consecutive measurements, at least 1 minute apart, with the person seated. Record BP twice daily (ideally morning and evening) for at least 4 days, and ideally for 7 days. **Discard the measurements taken on the first day** and use the average value of all the remaining measurements to confirm the diagnosis. --- ### 3. Staging of Hypertension Once ABPM or HBPM is completed, hypertension is classified into the following stages: | Stage | Clinic BP Threshold | ABPM / HBPM Average Threshold | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Stage 1 Hypertension** | **140/90 mmHg** to **159/99 mmHg** | **135/85 mmHg** to **149/94 mmHg** | | **Stage 2 Hypertension** | **160/100 mmHg** to **179/119 mmHg** | **≥ 150/95 mmHg** | | **Stage 3 (Severe) Hypertension** | **≥ 180 mmHg** systolic OR **≥ 120 mmHg** diastolic | *N/A (Assessed immediately in clinic)* | --- ### 4. Parallel Investigations (Target Organ Damage & Risk) While waiting for ABPM/HBPM confirmation, carry out investigations for **target organ damage** and **cardiovascular risk**: * **Cardiovascular Risk Assessment:** Use a formal assessment tool (such as **QRISK3**) to estimate 10-year cardiovascular risk. * **Urine:** Test for haematuria using a reagent strip, and send a urine sample to estimate the **albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR)** to check for proteinuria. * **Bloods:** Check **HbA1c** (diabetes), **electrolytes and creatinine / eGFR** (chronic kidney disease), and **total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol** (lipid profile). * **Eyes:** Perform **fundoscopy** to examine the retinas for hypertensive retinopathy. * **Heart:** Arrange a **12-lead ECG** to check for left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) or arrhythmias. --- ### 5. Handling Severe Hypertension (Clinic BP ≥ 180/120 mmHg) If a patient presents with a clinic BP of **180/120 mmHg or higher**, do not wait for ABPM/HBPM: 1. **Refer for same-day specialist review** if they have: * Signs of retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema (accelerated/malignant hypertension), **OR** * Life-threatening symptoms (e.g., new-onset confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, or acute kidney injury), **OR** * Suspected phaeochromocytoma (e.g., labile or postural hypotension, headache, palpitations, pallor, abdominal pain, or diaphoresis). 2. **If no same-day referral is needed:** Carry out target organ damage investigations immediately: * If **target organ damage is identified**, consider starting antihypertensive drug treatment **immediately**, without waiting for the results of ABPM or HBPM. * If **no target organ damage is identified**, repeat clinic BP measurement within 7 days, or confirm diagnosis using ABPM/HBPM. ``` ::: ::: ## Grounding with `ragnar` & `embed_google_gemini()` Instead of pasting all the NICE guideline into the prompt, `ragnar` chunks the document and uses `embed_google_gemini()` to index each chunk as a semantic vector in DuckDB: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ragnar) library(pdftools) chunks <- pdf_text(nice_url) |> paste(collapse = "\n") |> MarkdownDocument(origin = nice_url) |> markdown_chunk() store <- ragnar_store_create( location = ":memory:", embed = embed_google_gemini() ) ragnar_store_insert(store, chunks) ragnar_store_build_index(store) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_nice_rag <- chat$clone()$set_turns(list())$set_system_prompt("You are an expert clinical phenotyper.
